title: Ultrahigh-Power-Density Aluminum–Air Flow Battery Enabled by Electrolyte and Oxygen Transport Engineering
abstract: Abstract Aluminum–air batteries offer exceptionally high theoretical energy density and rely on an abundant, low-cost metal, but their practical deployment is limited by parasitic corrosion, incomplete aluminum utilization, and transport losses. Here, we report a membrane-free aluminum–air flow battery that couples a circulating alkaline electrolyte with stannate-assisted anode stabilization to enable high-power operation without an ion-conducting membrane. By systematically varying cathode oxidant, electrolyte flow rate, and aluminum purity, we show that electrolyte hydrodynamics and anode composition strongly govern cell resistance, interfacial polarization, and aluminum utilization. The optimized cell delivered a peak power density of 1.91 W/cm2 under oxygen operation, placing the oxygen-fed result among the highest reported for laboratory aluminum–air cells, while maintaining a peak power density of 0.63 W/cm2 under air. During galvanostatic discharge at 1000 mA/cm2, aluminum utilization reached 90%, with an aluminum-basis specific capacity of 2674 mAh/g and specific energy of 2840 Wh/kg. Electrochemical characterization revealed that enhanced electrolyte circulation reduces coupled ohmic, interfacial, and transport-associated losses, while aluminum purity strongly influences the evolving anode–electrolyte interface. These results establish membrane-free electrolyte management as an effective strategy for simultaneously achieving high power and efficient aluminum utilization, advancing mechanically rechargeable aluminum–air systems toward practical high-power energy storage.

title: Towards Scalable High-Voltage Battery Packs: A Modular Architecture Enabled by Dual Active Bridge Converters
abstract: The growing adoption of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) has increased the demand for scalable architectures that convert low-voltage (LV) battery packs into high-voltage (HV) configurations. However, series connection of LV packs is limited by the voltage ratings of their embedded Battery Management System (BMS) and protection circuitry. This paper proposes a modular Smart Battery architecture based on isolated Dual Active Bridge (DAB) DC–DC converters, which provide galvanic isolation, bidirectional power flow and independent voltage regulation for each LV battery module, allowing commercial LV packs to be integrated into an HV DC-link without hardware modifications. A master BMS controller performs State of Charge (SoC) balancing by adjusting the individual DAB output-voltage references through a proportional balancing law, while local proportional–integral (PI) controllers regulate the module output voltages. Functional performance was evaluated through PLECS simulations and controller hardware-in-the-loop (C-HIL) tests with four modules forming a 192-V dc link. The results demonstrate dc-link regulation under load transients and SoC equalization under the evaluated initial imbalances and capacity mismatches, supporting the coordinated-control implementation on the physical DSP against the real-time power-stage model.

title: THE SALAHI ACUTE RECOVERY CAPSULE (SARC) A Deployable Aerial Surgical and Intensive-Care System for Disaster and Conflict Zones
abstract: Author's Note Every day I work, bit by bit, on a different innovation, a different thought, or a different equation. Some days the pieces seem unrelated. After a year, they begin to line up, and what looked like scattered notes turns out to be a set of complete and coherent designs. I believe that anyone who truly wants to create something can attempt it. Formal permission is not the starting point; persistence is. This design is close to my heart because it brings health care to the doorstep of people who need it most. Surgical wards and intensive-care beds are among the most expensive things a society builds, and they are usually the first things lost when an earthquake, a flood, or a war arrives. The Salahi Acute Recovery Capsule (SARC) turns that relationship around. Instead of asking a critically injured person to survive the journey to a hospital, SARC sends the hospital to the person. Thousands of units can be carried by cargo aircraft and heavy helicopters toward a disaster or conflict zone, released close to the people who need them, and flown the last stretch on their own. When the work is done, they fly back into their carrier pods to be recharged, restocked, and sent out again. Each unit learns. Every operation that a remote surgeon performs through a SARC capsule becomes a lesson for the system's artificial intelligence, which watches, records, and gradually earns the right to perform proven tasks on its own. In practice this means that one doctor, sitting at a laptop on another continent, could oversee the diagnostics of many capsules at once while giving direct intensive care to a child in Ukraine, or in any other war zone or disaster field where no surgeon is available. To complete the picture, I have written SARC as a real speculative engineering blueprint, grounded in science rather than science fiction. Every major part is tied to an existing technology, a published clinical practice, or a measurable open question. I invite readers to check the detail of this work, to study it, to research it, and to add to it. SARC is one of the first engineering designs for a self-flying, deployable surgical ward that operates at the point of injury, and it is written so that it can become a prototype if its clinical components pass testing as well as I believe they will. Kaveh Dimitri Salahi Toronto, Ontario, Canada 23 November 2026 How to Read This Blueprint This document is written for two audiences at once. It is meant to be precise enough for a university researcher to test and cite, and plain enough for a donor, a policy maker, or a member of the public to follow from beginning to end. Technical terms are explained the first time they appear. Numbers are given with the reasoning behind them, so that a reader can check them rather than take them on trust. Five words carry a specific meaning throughout. A concept is a design or operating idea. A requirement is a condition that a part of the system must meet before testing or use can continue. A design reference is a number used for engineering planning; it is a starting point for testing, not a proven medical limit. An open question is a scientific or engineering uncertainty that needs evidence. A release gate is a measured pass-or-stop checkpoint that prevents the system from moving to its next stage until safety has been shown. Three rules organise every part of SARC. First, remove or isolate harmful material before connecting anything new. Second, put the needed support in place before the event it is meant to support. Third, define and validate a measurement before that measurement is allowed to control a treatment. SARC is a theoretical engineering blueprint and a public technical disclosure. It is not a clinical protocol, a treatment recommendation, a medical device specification, or a regulatory submission. The complete system has not been built, tested, or approved for use in people or animals. Rather than repeat this caution in every paragraph, the document states it once here and again, in full, in the closing section on engineering status and limits. All temperatures, flow rates, dimensions, durations, and pressures in this document are design references unless clearly stated otherwise, and none of them may be used as a treatment setting. SARC in Brief SARC is a flying, self-contained surgical and intensive-care unit for disaster and conflict zones. A single Surgical Group is made of five spheres, each about 8 feet (2.44 metres) across, joined in a line by magnets and mechanical couplers. From one end to the other, the spheres hold fuel and a generator, fluids and a water-purification plant, the patient capsule, surgical and medical supplies, and a battery. Each sphere carries four arms with four heavy-lift turbines on each arm, so every sphere can fly on its own if the group must separate. Large cargo aircraft carry SARC units in carrier pods to the nearest working airport. Heavy helicopters carry those pods into the affected region and set them down. The units then fly up to about 100 kilometres to reach injured people, land, and unfold. The capsule sphere opens, like folding paper in reverse, into a cylinder about 6 feet across and 8 feet long, holding a rotating patient cradle and a sealed bath. The patient lies in warm fluid with the head out through a soft neck seal, supported, monitored, and connected to separate circuits for blood, brain fluid, and gut support. Robotic arms, controlled by a remote surgeon and assisted by artificial intelligence, operate on the patient while the wound stays submerged. The bath water is made on site from local water that is filtered, purified, and tested before use, which removes the need to fly hundreds of kilograms of water. Fluids that enter the body are carried sterile. A planning simulation in this document estimates that most trauma patients reach a stable state for transfer in about three to four days, and that severe brain injuries and burns may take up to about eight days. Long-term brain recovery work, described in earlier SARC drafts, continues afterwards at fixed SARC Hub hospitals. SARC is deployed to designated civilian-affected zones. Inside those zones it treats everyone in need according to medical urgency, carries no weapons, and protects its data and hardware against capture. It is designed to be tested first on computer models, synthetic tissue, lab-grown human tissue, donated bodies, and donated organs, before any use in a living patient. Part I — The Aerial System 1. Why the Hospital Must Travel Modern trauma care rests on a simple observation: the sooner a severely injured person receives bleeding control, oxygen, and surgery, the more likely that person is to survive. Trauma systems in wealthy cities shorten this delay with ambulances, helicopters, and nearby trauma centres. In a large earthquake, a flood, or a war, that chain breaks. Roads close, hospitals are damaged or overwhelmed, staff are injured or displaced, and the number of patients can exceed local capacity many times over. Mobile medicine already exists in several forms. Air ambulances carry intensive care between hospitals. Field hospitals made of tents and containers are flown into disaster zones. A fully equipped eye hospital has been built inside an aircraft. Each of these brings care closer, but each still depends on runways, roads, large teams on the ground, or days of set-up. SARC asks a different question: what if the surgical ward itself could fly the final distance, land beside the patient, make its own water, power itself, and be operated by surgeons anywhere in the world? The SARC design answers that question by joining three lines of earlier work. The first is the acute recovery capsule described in SARC Extension E2.1 and Draft 5.0: a sealed, temperature-controlled bath environment with separate internal circuits, localised probes, and submerged robotic surgery. The second is heavy-lift unmanned aircraft, which in 2026 can lift payloads in the range of 150 to 200 kilograms per aircraft in commercial service. The third is remote and AI-assisted surgery, in which robotic instruments controlled from a distance are increasingly supported by machine learning trained on recorded operations. 2. The Deployment Chain SARC reaches a disaster through a three-layer chain, because no single aircraft type can do every part of the journey well. In the first layer, large fixed-wing cargo aircraft carry SARC units, packed inside carrier pods, from manufacturing and storage sites to the nearest working airport or airstrip. Fixed-wing aircraft are the most efficient way to move heavy loads across long distances. In the second layer, heavy-lift helicopters move the carrier pods from the airport into the affected region. The largest helicopter in service today, the Mil Mi-26, can lift a payload of up to 20 tonnes, and the largest Western heavy-lift helicopter, the Sikorsky CH-53K King Stallion, has completed external lifts of about 16 tonnes. If one complete Surgical Group weighs about one to one and a half tonnes, a single heavy helicopter can carry roughly ten to twenty units in one pod. Thousands of units therefore arrive through fleets of helicopters and repeated trips, not through any single aircraft. In the third layer, the SARC units fly themselves out of the pod and travel up to about 100 kilometres to the injured. The pod stays on the ground as a temporary base, relay station, and landing point. The earliest version of this design imagined units flying back into a passing cargo aircraft in mid-air. Cargo aircraft fly far faster than multirotor craft can, even at their slowest safe speed, so mid-air capture is not part of the first design. A hovering helicopter could in principle receive units, but the violent downwash under a large rotor would throw small craft off course. SARC therefore uses the carrier pod. title: Adaptive Fuzzy Balancing Control for Vehicle-Mounted Battery Strings Based on a Hierarchical Buck–Boost Topology
abstract: Cell-to-cell inconsistency remains a critical engineering bottleneck for lithium-ion battery strings in vehicle-mounted energy storage systems and is especially acute in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) auxiliary storage packs, where gravimetric energy density, charging turnaround, and balancing precision directly govern mission endurance and payload capacity. Conventional single-layer adjacent Buck–Boost topologies suffer from long energy transfer paths, high cumulative losses, and slow convergence under severe mismatch. This work pairs an improved hierarchical bidirectional Buck–Boost topology with a multi-constraint adaptive fuzzy controller. The two-layer shared-bus topology enables direct inter-module energy transfer with minimal additional components, while the controller takes SOC deviation as its primary input, embeds terminal voltage as a safety boundary in the fuzzy rule base, and tunes equalization intensity via a standard-deviation adaptive gain. Simulations on an 8-cell, 2-module system show that intra-module convergence time (max cell-to-cell SOC deviation ≤3%) falls by an average of 47% versus the conventional baseline. The fuzzy controller further reduces convergence time by 32.7% (35.0% for Module 1, 30.4% for Module 2) and shortens full-charging time by 15.4% (from ~1300 s to 1100 s) relative to the topology-only scheme, supporting its potential for vehicle-mounted battery management applications.
title_zh: Adaptive Fuzzy Balancing Control for Vehicle-Mounted Battery Strings Based on a Hierarchical Buck–Boost Topology
